content: 1. National infection prevention and control (IPC) programs must be integrated with other relevant national programs and professional organizations to ensure a comprehensive approach to combating antimicrobial resistance (AMR). These programs should have clearly defined objectives, functions, and responsibilities, with designated infection preventionists to oversee their implementation. 2. The minimum objectives of national IPC programs should include: Setting specific goals for managing endemic and epidemic infections. Developing evidence-based recommendations for IPC processes and practices that are proven to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and limit the spread of AMR. 3. The International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005) and the WHO Global Action Plan on AMR (2015) emphasize the importance of IPC as a core component of health system capacity building and preparedness. This includes creating national plans to prevent HAIs, strengthening national IPC policies and standards, and monitoring adherence to these policies. 4. National IPC programs should include the following components: A technical team of trained infection preventionists, including medical and nursing professionals, with formal IPC training and allocated time for their tasks. Authority for the technical team to make decisions and influence field implementation. A dedicated and protected budget for planned IPC activities, supported by national authorities and leaders. Strong linkages between the national IPC program and other related programs to ensure coordination and sustainability. 5. Evidence-based IPC guidelines should be developed and implemented to reduce HAIs and AMR. These guidelines must be adapted to local conditions for effective implementation and should reference international or national standards. Monitoring adherence to these guidelines is essential. 6. IPC education and training should be provided to all healthcare workers using participatory, team-based strategies, including bedside and simulation training. This training should be part of a broader health facility education strategy, including orientation for new employees and continuous education for existing staff, regardless of their role or position. 7. National IPC programs should support the development of pregraduate and postgraduate IPC curricula in collaboration with academic institutions. These curricula should reference international standards and be adapted to national needs and available resources. 8. Surveillance of HAIs is critical to guide IPC strategies. Surveillance systems should be based on national recommendations and tailored to the facility's resources. They should provide data on infection incidence, AMR patterns, high-risk populations, and the effectiveness of interventions. Quality microbiology and laboratory capacity are essential for reliable surveillance. 9. National HAI surveillance systems should integrate with public health infection surveillance systems and provide timely reports to decision-makers and frontline healthcare workers. These systems require government support, standardized case definitions, and mechanisms for data analysis and quality evaluation. 10. Multimodal strategies should be implemented at healthcare facilities to improve IPC practices and reduce HAIs and AMR. These strategies should involve organizational culture change, the engagement of champions or role models, and alignment with quality improvement programs. 11. Regular monitoring and auditing of IPC practices, with timely feedback to healthcare workers and management, are essential to drive behavior change and improve care quality. Sharing audit results with all stakeholders, including hospital management, is critical for achieving both individual and organizational improvements. 12. National IPC monitoring and evaluation programs should assess adherence to standards and the effectiveness of activities. Hand hygiene monitoring with feedback should be a key performance indicator. Regular reporting on national goals and strategies is necessary to document progress and guide interventions. 13. In acute healthcare facilities, bed occupancy should not exceed the standard capacity, and staffing levels should be adequate to meet patient workload. Proper spacing between patient beds must be maintained to reduce the risk of HAIs and AMR spread. In exceptional circumstances where bed capacity is exceeded, hospital management must ensure appropriate staffing and spacing. 14. The built environment, materials, and equipment in healthcare facilities must support IPC practices. This includes ensuring proper design, maintenance, and availability of resources to minimize infection risks.
